data.name: Moon osculating orbit info
text:
Moon (osculating orbit)
r = 0.002476 AU (3.704e+05 km)
x = -0.000332 AU, y = 0.002447 AU, z = 0.000173 AU

inner_core.name: Inner Core
inner_core.description: A solid ball of iron and nickel at Earth's center, nearly at its melting point despite the crushing pressure.
inner_core.about: Temperatures near 5,400 degrees Celsius keep the inner core close to melting even under the weight of the whole planet. It turns slightly faster than the rest of Earth, which adds complexity to the magnetic field generated in the liquid layer above it.
inner_core.source: Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), Preliminary Reference Earth Model, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297

outer_core.name: Outer Core
outer_core.description: A liquid layer of iron and nickel whose churning currents generate Earth's magnetic field.
outer_core.about: The outer core is molten iron and nickel with lighter elements mixed in, at 4,500 to 5,400 degrees Celsius. Convection in this conducting fluid acts as a dynamo, the geodynamo, and produces the magnetic field that reaches out into space to form the magnetosphere.
outer_core.source: Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), Preliminary Reference Earth Model, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297

lower_mantle.name: Lower Mantle
lower_mantle.description: The deep layer of hot, solid rock between the core and the upper mantle, flowing very slowly over millions of years.
lower_mantle.about: The lower mantle is solid silicate rock rich in iron and magnesium, at 2,200 to 4,500 degrees Celsius and under enormous pressure. Although solid, it creeps slowly by convection, and that slow flow is what drives the plates at the surface.
lower_mantle.source: Ishii, Huang, Myhill et al. (2019), Nature Geoscience 12:869-872 -- the sharp 660-km discontinuity; the global average depth of 660 +/- 10 km is from the same group's open companion, Ishii et al. (2018), Scientific Reports 8:6358

upper_mantle.name: Upper Mantle
upper_mantle.description: The rock beneath the crust, including the partly molten layer where most magma is born and on which the plates slide.
upper_mantle.about: The upper mantle includes the asthenosphere, a partly molten layer that flows more readily than the mantle below it, letting the tectonic plates move. It reaches from the base of the crust down to the top of the lower mantle, with temperatures from about 500 to 2,200 degrees Celsius.
upper_mantle.source: Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), Preliminary Reference Earth Model, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297 -- Moho

crust.name: Crust
crust.description: Earth's thin, solid outer skin: the ground we live on, the ocean floors, and everything that has ever lived.
crust.about: The crust is thin compared with the planet: 5 to 10 km under the oceans, where it is mostly basalt, and 30 to 50 km under the continents, where it is mostly granite. Surface temperatures range from about minus 80 to 60 degrees Celsius. It holds all known life and every resource we can reach.
crust.source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Earth -- volumetric mean radius, 6371.000 km. The Earth radius used as a unit is the equatorial radius: Prsa et al. (2016), AJ 152:41, on IAU 2015 Resolution B3 -- an Earth radius not qualified as equatorial or polar is the equatorial one, following common usage.
crust.note: Drawn at the mean radius, the sphere the interior layers (PREM) are measured against (Tony, 2026-09-28). Crust thickness (5-10 km oceanic, 30-50 km continental) is below the drawn resolution.
crust.radius_note: This is Earth's mean radius: the radius of a ball with the same volume as the smooth, slightly flattened shape fitted to sea level. The Earth radius used as a unit here is the equatorial radius, as the International Astronomical Union recommends, so the mean radius is a little less than one. The ground itself rises and falls from this by kilometres.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

lower_atmosphere.name: Lower Atmosphere (to the stratopause)
lower_atmosphere.description: The air where weather happens and the ozone layer sits: the troposphere and stratosphere, holding nearly all the atmosphere's mass.
lower_atmosphere.about: The troposphere, the lowest 12 km or so, is where clouds and weather form; above it the stratosphere, to about 50 km, holds the ozone layer. Together they contain 99 percent of the atmosphere's mass, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Temperature falls from about 15 degrees Celsius at sea level to minus 60 at the top of the troposphere, then warms again toward the stratopause as ozone absorbs sunlight.
lower_atmosphere.source: NOAA JetStream, "Layers of the Atmosphere"; NASA, "Earth's Atmospheric Layers" -- stratopause at about 50 km
lower_atmosphere.note: Troposphere and stratosphere, 99% of atmospheric mass. Drawn at the physical boundary since 2026-09-07 (L-295); before that at a visibility fraction its own hover contradicted.

upper_atmosphere.name: Upper Atmosphere (to the thermopause)
upper_atmosphere.description: The thin upper air where meteors burn up, the aurora glows, and the Space Station orbits, fading toward space.
upper_atmosphere.about: Above 50 km lie the mesosphere, where most meteors burn up, the thermosphere, where the aurora appears and the International Space Station flies, and, higher still, the beginning of the exosphere. In the thermosphere the gas can reach 2,000 degrees Celsius, yet it is so thin it would feel cold to the skin.
upper_atmosphere.source: NOAA JetStream, "Layers of the Atmosphere"; NASA, "Earth's Atmospheric Layers" -- thermosphere to about 600 km
upper_atmosphere.note: Mesosphere and thermosphere. The thermopause moves with solar activity over roughly 500-1,000 km; 600 km is the nominal figure.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

geocorona.name: Exosphere / Geocorona (hydrogen halo, detected extent)
geocorona.description: A faint halo of hydrogen gas that surrounds Earth and thins out far into space, the outermost trace of the atmosphere.
geocorona.about: The exosphere has no top: it simply thins into space. Its hydrogen glows faintly in ultraviolet light, a halo called the geocorona. This shell is drawn where that glow has been detected, not where the atmosphere ends.
geocorona.source: Baliukin, Bertaux, Quemerais, Izmodenov & Schmidt (2019), J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics 124:861, doi:10.1029/2018JA026136 -- the hydrogen geocorona is detected to at least 100 Earth radii
geocorona.note: The exosphere has no boundary: it thins into space. This shell is the sourced DETECTION FLOOR, not an edge, and it encloses the Moon's orbit at about 60 Earth radii.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

leo_inner.name: Low Earth Orbit, inner edge (200 km)
leo_inner.description: The lower edge of low Earth orbit, the band of space where most satellites and the Space Station fly.
leo_inner.about: Low Earth orbit is the region from roughly 200 to 2,000 km up. Satellites there circle at every angle to the equator, so together they form a shell around Earth rather than a ring, and each completes an orbit in about 90 to 120 minutes. The International Space Station, the Hubble Space Telescope, Starlink and most weather and Earth-observing satellites live here; the moving lights seen at dusk and dawn are usually these.
leo_inner.source: Drawing floor: the LEO region begins at the surface (IADC-02-01 Rev. 3); 200 km marks where orbits stop decaying within days. Declared, not measured.

leo_outer.name: Low Earth Orbit, outer edge (2,000 km)
leo_outer.description: The upper edge of low Earth orbit, about 2,000 km up, above which the sky belongs to higher orbits.
leo_outer.about: Low Earth orbit is the region from roughly 200 to 2,000 km up. Satellites there circle at every angle to the equator, so together they form a shell around Earth rather than a ring, and each completes an orbit in about 90 to 120 minutes. The International Space Station, the Hubble Space Telescope, Starlink and most weather and Earth-observing satellites live here; the moving lights seen at dusk and dawn are usually these.
leo_outer.source: IADC Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines, IADC-02-01 Rev. 3 (June 2021), sec. 3.3.2 -- the LEO Protected Region extends to 2,000 km altitude

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

geostationary_ring.name: Geostationary Belt (GEO)
geostationary_ring.description: A ring of satellites 35,786 km above the equator that circle exactly as fast as Earth turns, so each hangs over one spot.
geostationary_ring.about: Satellites in the geostationary belt orbit once a day, matching Earth's rotation, and so stay fixed over a point on the equator. Several hundred of them carry television, weather imagery and communications for much of the world. In April 2029 the asteroid Apophis will pass inside this ring, a few thousand kilometers below the nearest satellites.
geostationary_ring.hover: A ring in the equatorial plane, not a sphere: satellites here keep pace with Earth's turning and hang over one longitude.
geostationary_ring.source: Derived: (GM_E / omega^2)^(1/3) from IERS Conventions (2010) TN36 Table 1.1 -- GM_E = 3.986004418e14 m^3 s^-2, nominal mean angular velocity 7.292115e-5 rad s^-1. The hover's sentence on keeping pace: NASA Earth Observatory, Riebeek (2009, page updated 2025-11-14), Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits, section High Earth Orbit, https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/catalog-of-earth-satellite-orbits/ -- at 42,164 km from Earth's centre the orbit matches Earth's rotation, so a satellite seems to stay over a single longitude; circular and over the equator, it is geostationary, always over the same place (read 2026-10-06).
geostationary_ring.note: A ring in the equatorial plane, not a sphere, tilted with Earth's equator by the served pole. 42,164 km from Earth's centre, 35,786 km up.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

params._comment: The orrery emits magnetopause, bow shock, inner belt and outer belt from ONE call. Served as four rows: the two standoffs here, the two belts in van_allen_belts. Renderer for the standoff shapes is step 3.

magnetopause.name: Magnetopause
magnetopause.description: The outer boundary of Earth's magnetic field, where it holds off the solar wind: pressed in by day, trailing a long tail by night.
magnetopause.about: Earth's magnetic field carves a cavity in the solar wind called the magnetosphere. On the side facing the Sun the wind presses it in; on the night side it stretches into a magnetotail observed far beyond the Moon's distance. The magnetopause is that boundary. It deflects the solar wind and turns aside many of the charged particles that reach Earth from the Sun and from beyond the solar system. The surface drawn is a model for a quiet solar wind; the real boundary moves in and out as the wind's pressure changes.

surface._model: Shue et al. (1998) eq. 10 with eq. 11. r = r0 [2 / (1 + cos theta)]^alpha, theta measured from the Sun-Earth line, r0 the standoff below. The geometry evaluates alpha = (a6 + a7 Bz)(1 + a8 ln Dp) from the rows here; alpha gets no row of its own because no text on the page prints it. At the declared conditions alpha is 0.59 -- two figures, because a6 is 0.58 +/- 0.01 and that carries straight through.

a6.source: Shue et al. (1998), doi:10.1029/98JA01103 -- Table 1 (After Fit) row a6, p. 17,698: 0.58 +/- 0.01. The leading term of eq. 11.

a7.source: Shue et al. (1998), doi:10.1029/98JA01103 -- Table 1 (After Fit) row a7, p. 17,698: -0.007 +/- 0.0005 per nT. Eq. 11 prints it as a subtraction; the table carries the sign, so this value is negative and adds.

a8.source: Shue et al. (1998), doi:10.1029/98JA01103 -- Table 1 (After Fit) row a8, p. 17,698: 0.024 +/- 0.0004. The pressure term of eq. 11.

bz._declared: A neutral midpoint chosen for this scene, NOT a figure from the paper. Both boundaries are evaluated at the same conditions so the two surfaces can be compared.

pressure._declared: The solar wind dynamic pressure both fits are evaluated at. Declared for this scene, not measured.

cut_angle._declared: Where the drawn surface stops, measured from the nose. Shue's surface has no end: at this flaring the radius grows without bound as theta approaches 180 degrees, so a drawing must choose a stop. Shue et al. (1998) fig. 6, p. 17,695 plots the model out to 120 degrees, the furthest the authors evaluate it. A drawing limit, not an edge.

magnetopause.hover:
Shue et al. (1998), for the solar wind assumed here:
Bz {bz} nT, dynamic pressure {pressure} nPa
Drawn to {cut_angle} deg from the nose, as far as the paper plots its model. Beyond that angle the boundary is drawn as the magnetotail.
Not tilted: the model is symmetric about the Sun line.
magnetopause.source: Shue et al. (1998), J. Geophys. Res. 103:17691, doi:10.1029/98JA01103 -- eq. 10 evaluated at the declared conditions (Bz = 0 nT, Dp = 2 nPa). Corroboration: Lugaz et al. (2016), doi:10.1038/ncomms13001 -- typical subsolar magnetopause 9-11 R_E, which contains this.
magnetopause.note: Quiet-time nominal. Under storm compression it can fall inside geostationary orbit (6.6 R_E).

bow_shock.name: Bow Shock
bow_shock.description: The shock wave where the supersonic solar wind first slows as it hits Earth's magnetic field, like the bow wave of a boat.
bow_shock.about: The solar wind moves faster than sound travels through the thin gas of space, so when it meets Earth's magnetic field it cannot flow smoothly around it: a standing shock forms upstream, sunward of the magnetopause, where the wind slows and heats. The surface drawn is a model for a quiet solar wind, and real crossings scatter around it.

surface._model: Jelinek et al. (2012), the paraboloid of eqs. 15-16 parameterised by tau: x = R0 p^(-1/eps) - tau^2 / 2, and the distance from the Sun-Earth line is sqrt(2 R0 p^(-1/eps)) tau / lambda. At tau = 0 this is the standoff below. A different functional form from the magnetopause because it is a different paper's fit, not a variation on Shue.

r0.source: Jelinek, Nemecek and Safrankova (2012), J. Geophys. Res. 117:A05208, doi:10.1029/2011JA017252 -- eq. 14, p. 5: R_BS = 15.02 p^(-1/6.55), so 15.02 R_E is the bow shock standoff at p = 1 nPa.

epsilon.source: Jelinek et al. (2012), doi:10.1029/2011JA017252 -- eq. 14, p. 5: the pressure exponent of R_BS = 15.02 p^(-1/6.55).

lambda.source: Jelinek et al. (2012), doi:10.1029/2011JA017252 -- sec. 4, in the text after eq. 11: lambda = 1.17 for the bow shock. Their magnetopause lambda of 1.54 is deliberately not used here, because this page's magnetopause is Shue's.

pressure._declared: The same declared pressure as the magnetopause. Both surfaces must be evaluated at the same conditions or their relative positions mean nothing.

cut_angle._declared: Where the drawn surface stops, measured from the nose. Jelinek et al. fitted crossings within 7 hours of local noon either side, and 7 hours of Earth's turn is 105 degrees. A drawing limit set by where the data was, not by where the formula fails -- the opposite reason from the magnetopause's 120.

bow_shock.hover:
Jelinek et al. (2012), at dynamic pressure {pressure} nPa
Drawn to {cut_angle} deg from the nose, which is how far round the crossings the fit was made from actually reached.
That is where the drawing stops, not where the shock ends.
Not tilted: the fit is symmetric about the Sun line.
bow_shock.source: Jelinek, Nemecek and Safrankova (2012), J. Geophys. Res. 117:A05208, doi:10.1029/2011JA017252 -- eq. 14, R_BS = 15.02 p^(-1/6.55), evaluated at the declared pressure of 2 nPa. The paper states no uncertainty on its fitted numbers; how far real crossings fall from the fit (fig. 7) is given in the hover. Corroboration: Lugaz et al. (2016), Nat. Commun. 7:13001, doi:10.1038/ncomms13001 -- 11-14 R_E subsolar under normal solar wind, which contains this.
bow_shock.note: Quiet-time nominal, at the same declared solar wind pressure as the magnetopause. An earlier note here cited Farris & Russell (1994) for the model FORM; that was a miscitation -- it is a relation for the standoff at a given Mach number and takes obstacle shape as an input, not a shape model. Removed 2026-09-12 (L-305).

magnetotail.name: Magnetotail
magnetotail.description: Earth's magnetic field, drawn out by the solar wind into a long tail on the night side.
magnetotail.about: The solar wind drags Earth's magnetic field out behind the planet into a long tail. Spacecraft crossing it far downstream found that it stops widening about 120 Earth radii behind Earth and is about 60 Earth radii across beyond there. ISEE-3 followed it out to 220 Earth radii, which is how far the spacecraft went rather than where the tail ends. The tail is drawn round, which is close to its shape on average; at any moment it is often flattened, in a direction set by the solar wind's own magnetic field, which keeps changing.
magnetotail._declared: The tail continues Shue's magnetopause surface from where the drawing of that surface stops, at the magnetopause's served cut angle; its starting distance and radius are worked out in the page from the served Shue rows, not served. From there it widens in a straight line to drawn_radius at flare_end, then keeps that radius to drawn_end, and it is round. flare_end and diameter are measurements; drawn_radius and drawn_end are rules over them, declared on their rows in constants_new.py, and the page uses them only for the shape. The five numbers the orrery's tail was drawn with until 2026-09-25 (100, 15 and 25 Earth radii, colour and opacity), which nothing in the gallery read, are gone (L-322 Stage D, gallery patch 3). color and opacity here are drawing choices, the magnetopause's, so the two read as one surface.

flare_end.source: Slavin, Smith, Sibeck, Baker, Zwickl and Akasofu (1985), 'An ISEE 3 study of average and substorm conditions in the distant magnetotail', J. Geophys. Res. 90(A11):10875, doi:10.1029/JA090iA11p10875 -- abstract: flaring ceases on average at |X| = 120 +/- 10 R_E.

diameter.source: Slavin et al. (1985), doi:10.1029/JA090iA11p10875 -- abstract: from 756 magnetopause crossings, a low-latitude magnetotail diameter of 60 +/- 5 R_E at |X| = 130 - 225 R_E.
diameter.note: Low-latitude: the crossings were near the plane of Earth's orbit, so this is the tail's width, side to side, not its height.

drawn_radius._declared: Half the measured diameter, the radius of the round tube the tail is drawn as beyond flare_end. A rule, not a measurement; its reasons are on the row in constants_new.py.

drawn_end._declared: Where the drawing stops: equal to observed_extent, how far ISEE-3 went. A drawing limit, not an edge of anything physical.

observed_extent.source: Slavin, Tsurutani, Smith, Jones and Sibeck (1983), 'Average configuration of the distant (less than 220-earth-radii) magnetotail - Initial ISEE-3 magnetic field results', Geophys. Res. Lett. 10(10):973, doi:10.1029/GL010i010p00973 -- the abstract states that the magnetotail retains much of its near-Earth structure out to X = -220 Earth radii. Abstract open at ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19830066648. The same abstract's figures for where flaring ends and for the tail's diameter are superseded by the same mission's 1985 averages, served here as flare_end and diameter.
observed_extent.note: Read as OBSERVED TO AT LEAST, not as an edge. 220 R_E is ISEE-3's reach on its first two tail passes, so the figure is bounded by the orbit rather than by where the tail ends. Two further signatures are more distant and less like a tail: Ness, Scearce and Cantarano (1967), doi:10.1029/JZ072i015p03769, report Pioneer 7 in the expected tail region at 900 to 1,050 R_E over a week in 1966, intermittently and with no coherent tail, the title saying 'probable'; and Intriligator et al. (1979), Geophys. Res. Lett. 6:585, report tail-ASSOCIATED phenomena near 3,100 R_E, read by later work as signatures disconnected from Earth.

magnetotail.hover:
The straight widening up to that point is our choice; the measurements give only its two ends.
The drawing stops at {observed_extent} Earth radii, which is how far the spacecraft went, not where the tail ends.
Drawn round, its average shape; at any moment it is often flattened.
magnetotail.source: Slavin et al. (1985), J. Geophys. Res. 90(A11):10875, doi:10.1029/JA090iA11p10875 -- ISEE-3: flaring ceases on average at 120 +/- 10 R_E behind Earth, and the tail is 60 +/- 5 R_E across beyond there. Slavin et al. (1983), Geophys. Res. Lett. 10(10):973, doi:10.1029/GL010i010p00973 -- observed to 220 R_E. The tail's shape: Sibeck and Lin (2014), J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics 119, doi:10.1002/2013JA019471 -- the distant tail is often flattened along the part of the solar wind's magnetic field that lies across the Sun-Earth line; Maezawa, Hori, Mukai, Saito, Yamamoto, Kokubun and Nishida (1997), Adv. Space Res. 20(4-5):949, doi:10.1016/S0273-1177(97)00503-6 -- GEOTAIL found the distant tail about the same size in both directions under average conditions.
magnetotail.note: The straight widening between where the Sun-facing surface stops and 120 Earth radii is our choice: the measurements give only its two ends.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

magnetic_tilt.source: Alken et al. (2021), International Geomagnetic Reference Field: the thirteenth generation, Earth Planets Space 73:49, doi:10.1186/s40623-020-01288-x -- the angle between the geomagnetic dipole axis and Earth's rotation axis at epoch 2020.0. The paper prints no tilt of its own: constants_new.py computes it from the paper's three degree-1 Gauss coefficients, the relation the paper gives for the geomagnetic poles, and serves it at five figures. It is decreasing by about 0.049 degrees a year (magnetic_tilt_rate, from the same coefficients' published rates), so any quotation of it carries its epoch. The belts' hover says the magnetic equator turns with Earth: the paper's Table 4 places the 2020.0 north geomagnetic pole at a point on Earth, 80.65 N, -72.68 E (constants_new.py, read 2026-09-21), so the dipole turns with the ground beneath it. This sentence said 'rounded to a tenth of a degree' and 'about 0.05 deg per decade' until 2026-09-26; the decade figure was ten times too small (L-322 Stage D, gallery patch 3).
magnetic_tilt.note: Served so the hover can quote it. The rings are NOT tilted by it. They are drawn in the equatorial plane, which is the daily average of the magnetic one, because a tilted plane needs a direction as well as an angle and that direction turns once a day while this scene is frozen (L-231, Tony's ruling 2026-09-15).

params._frame: The edge rows below are geocentric distances in the geomagnetic equatorial plane, which is the frame their sources state. Tony's ruling, 2026-09-14 (L-323 ruling B, second amendment). The literature is mixed -- Y. X. Li et al. (2023) states the outer span in L shells and Baker et al. (2018) states it both ways -- so each row names the paper its figure follows and the frame travels with the row rather than with the block.

inner_belt_distance.source: Baker et al. (2018), Space Sci. Rev. 214:17, doi:10.1007/s11214-017-0452-7 -- sec. 2, inner-zone proton fluxes peak near geocentric r ~ 1.5 R_E
inner_belt_distance.note: A flux PEAK, not an edge. The edges are their own rows below, as of 2026-09-14 (L-305 item 7); this note carried the span in prose until then, which is what let the served figure and the orrery's disagree.

inner_belt_inner_edge.source: Meredith, Horne, Kersten, Fraser and Grew (2014), J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics 119:5328, doi:10.1002/2014JA020064 -- introduction, first paragraph: the inner belt extends from about 1.1 to 2 Earth radii in the geomagnetic equatorial plane. Open full text at nora.nerc.ac.uk. Meredith states this as background and passes it on from Baker et al. (2007), which is the layer below rather than the source.
inner_belt_inner_edge.note: Koskinen and Kilpua (2022) sec. 1.1 corroborate 1.1 to 2 R_E but are NOT the source, because they state it for the inner ELECTRON belt and put the energetic protons over about 1.1 to 3 R_E. The figure matched and the scope did not.

inner_belt_outer_edge.source: Meredith et al. (2014), doi:10.1002/2014JA020064 -- introduction, first paragraph, the outer end of the same stated span.
inner_belt_outer_edge.note: Two rows rather than one span, because provenance is per number and the two edges do not move together.

outer_belt_distance.source: Li et al. (2025), J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics, doi:10.1029/2024JA033504 -- sec. 1, the outer belt is most intense around L = 4 and 5; the value served is our midpoint of that band. Kellerman et al. (2014), as reported in arXiv:1809.00902 -- maximum electron flux at L = 4-5; the arXiv paper is the document opened and Kellerman is the layer below it.
outer_belt_distance.note: A flux PEAK, not an edge. The unit is L, the McIlwain parameter, which equals geocentric distance in Earth radii only where a field line crosses the magnetic equator -- so any string printing this value says 'at the equator'. Baker et al. (2018) was removed from this citation on 2026-09-14: his figure 30 uses L* = 4.5 as a selected analysis location rather than a universal peak, and his span figure belongs on the edge row below.

outer_belt_inner_edge.source: Meredith et al. (2014), doi:10.1002/2014JA020064, and Li, Tu, Selesnick and Huang (2024), J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics 129:e2023JA032171, doi:10.1029/2023JA032171 -- both state the outer belt extending from 3 Earth radii, in their introductions. Open full text at nora.nerc.ac.uk and par.nsf.gov.
outer_belt_inner_edge.note: The layer below is Paulikas and Blake (1979) with Baker et al. (1986) for Meredith, and Ganushkina et al. (2011) with Van Allen et al. (1958) for Li. Baker et al. (2018) sec. 2 gives the same inner edge from SAMPEX and reports it reaching L ~ 2.5 under strong driving.

outer_belt_outer_edge.source: Meredith et al. (2014), doi:10.1002/2014JA020064, and Li, Tu et al. (2024), doi:10.1029/2023JA032171 -- both state the outer belt extending to 7 Earth radii, in their introductions.
outer_belt_outer_edge.note: The measuring review disagrees on the outside and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved by silence: Baker et al. (2018) sec. 2 and 3.4 puts the outer zone at r ~ 3 to >= 6.5 R_E from SAMPEX and, in L, at about 3.0 to 6.5. Koskinen and Kilpua (2022) sec. 1.1 put the outer reach at 7 to 10 R_E, which is why an outer figure near 10 R_E is not the physical impossibility one checker called it -- the belt's outer edge approaches the magnetopause, and magnetopause shadowing is a standard loss mechanism.

descriptions: A ring of trapped charged particles, mostly protons, held by Earth's magnetic field close above the atmosphere.
A broader ring of trapped electrons farther out, that swells and shrinks with solar storms.
abouts: The inner Van Allen belt is a region of energetic protons trapped by Earth's magnetic field. It follows the magnetic equator, which is tilted from the geographic one and turns with Earth once a day; the ring drawn here lies in the daily average of that plane.

The outer Van Allen belt is mostly energetic electrons, trapped farther out than the inner belt, and it swells and shrinks as the solar wind changes. Like the inner belt it follows the magnetic equator; the ring drawn is the daily average of that tilted plane.
hovers_band: Drawn at {drawn} Earth radii: halfway across the band, {low} to {high} Earth radii out at the magnetic equator, where the belt is most intense. The halfway point is our choice for the picture, not a measured peak.
hovers_rings: The belt is one continuous region; its evenly spaced rings only mark its extent, and the brighter ring marks where it is most intense.
The belt is one continuous region; its evenly spaced rings only mark its extent, and the brighter ring marks where it is most intense.
hovers_plane: The ring lies in Earth's equatorial plane, the daily average of the magnetic equator, which turns with Earth and in 2020 was tilted {tilt} degrees from it{rate} (IGRF-13 model).
The ring lies in Earth's equatorial plane, the daily average of the magnetic equator, which turns with Earth and in 2020 was tilted {tilt} degrees from it{rate} (IGRF-13 model).
params._declared: n_points, colours, names and info_borders are drawing choices; info_borders mirrors the orrery's two-standards outline (shell_configs.py). Each belt is drawn as rings evenly spaced from its served inner edge to its served outer edge, on the step that also lands on its served peak, so the number of rings follows from those rows and is not a setting; the peak ring is drawn brighter and larger. The typed belt_thickness of 0.5 Earth radii and n_rings of 5 were removed rather than promoted (L-322 Stage D, gallery patch 3; the orrery since patch D9).

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

hill_sphere.name: Hill Sphere (gravitational dominance over the Sun)
hill_sphere.description: The region where Earth's gravity, not the Sun's, is the stronger hold; the Moon orbits well inside it.
hill_sphere.about: Inside the Hill sphere a body can orbit Earth without being pulled away by the Sun. The Moon lies deep within it. Beyond this sphere the Sun's gravity wins, and an object would drift into its own orbit around the Sun.
hill_sphere.source: Derived: r_H = a (GM_E / 3 GM_Sun)^(1/3) with a = 1 AU; GM_E from IERS Conventions (2010) TN36 Table 1.1, GM_Sun from IAU 2015 Resolution B3
hill_sphere.note: About 1.50 million km. The Moon at about 60 Earth radii sits well inside it, which is why it stays bound. a = 1 AU exactly; Earth's semi-major axis is 1.00000011 AU (NASA Earth Fact Sheet).

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1

rotation_period.source: Derived in constants_new.py: one full turn divided by the nominal mean Earth angular velocity, 7.292115e-5 rad/s, of IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, Table 1.2 (the GRS80 parameters) -- the sidereal period, one turn measured against the stars.

params.source: The pole the room draws is Earth's north pole on the scene's date from JPL Horizons (observer quantity 32, target 399), served by the cache builder as pole_of_date. The pole here is the FALLBACK, drawn only when no pole of date is served: the z-axis of the ICRF, which IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, sec. 2.1.1, holds within about 0.02 arcseconds of Earth's mean pole at J2000.0, and which the Horizons manual's reference frames section describes as aligned with FK5/J2000 to that level. The IAU working group report (Archinal et al. 2018) was cited here until 2026-09-26; it gives no pole for Earth and sends users to the IERS.
params.note: Same shape as the Sun's orientation block; read by poleBasis(). The equator plane and the GEO ring both hang off this. rotation_period is quoted in the axis hover (L-322 Stage D, gallery patch 3).

tilt.derived: the angle between Earth's pole of date and the pole of the Earth-Moon barycenter's orbit of date, both turned into the ecliptic of J2000 by the frame angle
